title: FINN: agentic build log
purpose: How FINN, a secure mobile-first investment agent for Indian equities, was built with an AI coding agent: the prompts, the agent's replies, what it changed, and how each step was checked. Use it to teach how to direct an agent to build a safe, secure app from your own requirements.
how_to_read: Phases run in order: requirements, first build, iteration, features, security audit, deployment.
User prompts are written the way a skilled prompter would phrase them. Agent replies summarise what the agent said, did and verified.
The work, the findings and the verification results are the real ones from this build.
Deployment entries marked 'pending' are steps to run on the chosen host; their results are filled in when run.
prompting_principles: Open with the whole picture: stack, users, features, constraints and how you want the agent to work.
State non-negotiables explicitly: no secrets in the client, honest scraping, rules before models.
Ask for verification after every step, including what could not be checked.
Give one focused change per prompt, with a reference (a screenshot, a mockup, a checklist) where you have one.
Name the outcome, not the implementation, and let the agent propose how.
Ask for security as its own pass against a named checklist, then ask for proof, not claims.
Keep secrets out of the conversation: put keys in .env yourself and tell the agent they are there.

turns.prompt:
You are building FINN, a mobile-first investment agent for Indian equities (NSE and BSE). Work in this empty folder and build it end to end.

TECH STACK
- Frontend: React 18 + Vite, plain CSS, no UI library. Mobile first, works on a phone browser.
- Backend: Node.js + Express (ES modules). One process serves the API and the built client, so there is one thing to deploy.
- Database: MongoDB when MONGODB_URI is set; otherwise fall back to JSON files on disk, behind one storage interface. The app must run with no database and no API keys.
- Models: any OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint, keys only in backend/.env, never in the client.

USERS
A portfolio manager who holds 15 to 20 stocks and has no time to read every exchange filing.

PUSH (the Brief, the home screen)
1. Windowed digest of filings across the portfolio, default last 24 hours, selectable (3, 7, 30 days or two dates).
2. Prioritise: classify every filing by category and tier (material, worth a glance, routine). Collapse the same event filed on both exchanges into one item.
3. Results first cut: Revenue, EBITDA, PBT and PAT against the previous quarter and the same quarter last year.
4. Management changes: who, which post, effective date, and a short bio from the filing.
5. Triggered alerts: end-of-day price and volume thresholds the user sets, and material announcements.

PULL (Research)
For any NSE ticker, from primary sources only (annual reports, concall transcripts, reported financials):
snapshot, multi-year trajectory, balance sheet, cash-flow quality, narrative vs numbers, current guidance, bull vs bear, and promise vs delivered over the last four quarters, each promise with its verbatim quote and source call. Add a question box that answers with page-cited quotes.

EFFICIENCY (a hard requirement)
- Rules before models: classification, priority, charts and computed verdicts must not call a model.
- Two model tiers: a cheap fast model reads documents, a stronger model judges once.
- Cache every filed document forever (it never changes) and every model answer on a hash of its prompt.
- Send models only the relevant passages, not whole PDFs.

DATA SOURCES
Use public sources only and identify the client honestly. Do not spoof browser headers or bypass protections. Prefer the NSE announcements RSS feed, Screener.in company pages and a public price API with a fallback.

DESIGN
Clean, calm, readable on a phone. Numbers in a monospace face. Hand-drawn SVG charts. Every screen must answer "what needs my attention?" first.

DELIVERABLES
- Working app with run instructions in README.md.
- .env.example listing every setting; .gitignore that excludes .env and local data.
- A short note on design decisions and known limits.

HOW TO WORK
Plan first and tell me the plan in a few lines. Build in vertical slices. After each slice, verify against live data and tell me what you checked and what you could not check. Ask me only when a decision is genuinely mine.
turns.why_this_prompt_works: One complete brief: stack, users, every feature with acceptance detail, efficiency and data-source rules, deliverables, and a working method that demands verification.

turns.reply:
Plan: an Express backend with a storage layer (MongoDB or JSON files), source adapters (Screener, a price API, the NSE RSS feed), a rule-based classifier, a push module (digest, grouping, results card, bios) and a research module (computed facts, a background analysis job, Ask). Then a React client with three screens: Brief, Research, Rules.

Built in slices, each checked against live data. The NSE and BSE JSON APIs refuse automated clients, so filings come from the public NSE RSS feed, polled every five minutes and stored to build history, plus each company's BSE announcements via Screener. Without a model key everything rule-based works; the written analysis switches on when a key is added.
actions: Scaffolded backend (Express, ESM) and frontend (Vite + React).
store.js: one interface over MongoDB or JSON files; read-through cache with in-flight de-duplication and stale-on-error.
sources/: Screener parser (tables, announcements, annual reports, concalls), price quotes with fallback, NSE RSS poller.
classify.js: ordered regex rules giving 17 categories and three tiers, no model.
push.js: digest grouped by ticker, category and IST day; results first cut (QoQ/YoY); people extraction with regex fallback.
research.js: TTM, CAGRs, balance sheet, cash conversion, signals; background job reading 4 transcripts and 1 annual report with the fast tier, then one smart-tier verdict; Ask with cited quotes.
docs.js: PDF text extraction cached forever; keyword-scored passage selection instead of embeddings.
llm.js: fast and smart tiers over any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, prompt-hash cache, token ledger.
Client: Brief, Research and Rules screens; hand-drawn SVG sparkline and series charts with a scrub readout.
verification: 18 holdings priced from the live price API.
A 7-day digest classified and grouped; NSE feed items matched to holdings.
Results first cut checked against MARUTI's reported quarter.
Research facts computed for DIXON, HDFCBANK (bank metrics) and ETERNAL.
A 187-page annual report extracted in about 2 seconds.
Full model pipeline exercised against a local stand-in server before any paid key was used.

turns.prompt: Restyle the app to a light theme: white cards on a soft lavender wash, large radii, a compact floating dock. Make it installable as an app with a web manifest and a service worker. Also tell me plainly: is a model API key mandatory?

turns.prompt: Use dynamic viewport units (dvh) so the layout fits mobile browsers with collapsing toolbars. On the home screen keep only what needs attention today.

turns.prompt: I put a GLM gateway key in backend/.env as GLM_API_KEY. The analysis still says no model. Find out why and fix it. Do not print the key.

turns.reply: Two causes. First, the gateway needs its base URL, which was missing; the settings panel now names the exact missing variable instead of failing silently. Second, the model is a reasoning model: it spent its whole token allowance thinking and returned an empty answer. Fixed by requesting low reasoning effort and reserving extra tokens for thinking.
findings: GLM_BASE_URL unset, so the provider was skipped.
Empty content with finish_reason 'length' from the reasoning model.
Occasional trailing text after the JSON answer.
actions: llm.js: GLM preset requiring key and base URL; problem message surfaced in /api/meta.
reasoning_effort 'low' plus a think budget added to max_tokens; 180 s timeout; retry on 429 and 5xx.
Balanced-bracket JSON parser that takes the first complete object.
verification: Live Ask on DIXON answered in under 3 seconds with page-cited quotes.
Full DIXON analysis: credibility 'mixed', 6 promises, 3 bull and 3 bear points; about 31k fast-tier tokens on first read, 12 seconds when cached.

turns.prompt: The browser console shows: TypeError: Failed to execute 'clone' on 'Response': Response body is already used, at sw.js line 19. Explain it and fix it.

turns.reply: The service worker cloned each response only after the cache opened, by which time the page had already read the body. It now clones first, then caches. Cache version bumped so the old worker is replaced.

turns.prompt: Before this goes on the open internet, add an access lock so nobody can use the app or spend my model budget. Use a secret code from an environment variable for now; a real login page comes later, so keep the check in one place.

turns.reply: ACCESS_CODE in the backend env gates every API route. The app opens to a lock screen; the code is entered once per device and sent in a header. Comparison is constant time, and wrong codes are rate-limited per IP.
actions: server.js: /api/access and /api/unlock; gate on all other /api routes; codeOk() is the single swap point for future sessions.
10 wrong codes in 15 minutes blocks that IP, even for the right code.
Client: Lock screen, code stored per device, automatic return to the lock screen on any 401, 'Lock FINN on this device' in Rules.
Service worker never caches the access check.
Generated a random code into the git-ignored .env without printing it.

turns.prompt:
Run a security audit of the whole app against this checklist. For every item, report Pass, Fail or Not applicable with the evidence. Fix every Fail, then prove each fix against the running server. Do not print secrets.

1. Secrets and credentials
   - No API keys, tokens or passwords hardcoded; search the code and the full git history.
   - No secrets in client-side code or client environment variables.
   - Environment variables set in every environment; nothing fails silently when one is missing.
   - .gitignore excludes every .env file and none is tracked.
2. Authentication
   - Passwords hashed with a modern algorithm; sessions expire; strong signing secrets.
   - Reset tokens expire and are single use; email verification enforced; OAuth state validated.
3. Authorization
   - Every API route checks who the caller is; public routes return only public data.
   - Users can only reach their own data (test for IDOR by swapping ids).
   - Admin routes restricted; tenant boundaries enforced on the server.
4. Input validation
   - Parameterised queries, no string-built queries or operator injection.
   - Uploads restricted by type and size on the server.
   - User and model text escaped before rendering; no raw HTML injection.
5. Rate limiting
   - Login and reset endpoints rate-limited without permanent lockouts.
   - AI endpoints have per-user and overall spend limits.
6. Payments and webhooks
   - Webhook signatures verified; events processed once; access checked on the server.
7. Infrastructure
   - Row-level security where a database is exposed directly.
   - Error responses never leak stack traces, upstream URLs or file paths.

Also check: server-side request forgery, security headers, CORS, request size limits and dependency vulnerabilities.
turns.why_this_prompt_works: A named checklist turns 'make it secure' into testable items, and 'prove each fix' forces evidence instead of claims.

turns.reply: Audited all 25 items. Payments, uploads, accounts and SQL do not exist in FINN, so those items are not applicable and are listed as such. Secrets, client code, env handling and .gitignore passed. Five gaps found and fixed.
findings: Spend abuse: model endpoints had no limits, so anyone could run up the bill.
Error leakage: upstream error messages were returned to the browser verbatim.
Open CORS: any website could call the API from a visitor's browser.
Unvalidated ticker in the research route reached upstream URLs.
Dependency: the PDF library pulled in canvas -> tar with a critical path-traversal advisory.
Links taken from scraped pages could in theory carry javascript: URLs.
actions: llm.js: server-wide cap on fresh tokens per day (LLM_DAILY_TOKENS, default 2M); cached answers free.
server.js: per-IP limits (300/min on /api, 30 model calls per 10 min, 12 new analyses per hour; polling a running job is free).
server.js: CSP, X-Frame-Options DENY, nosniff, referrer and permissions policies, X-Powered-By removed.
server.js: CORS off unless CORS_ORIGIN lists an origin; JSON bodies capped at 50 kB; digest window bounded.
server.js: ticker route parameter validated; errors logged server-side, generic or allow-listed message to the client.
unpdf upgraded to 2.x (same API, no canvas or tar).
Client: safeUrl() lets only http(s) links render.
verification: npm audit --omit=dev: 0 vulnerabilities in both packages.
Ticker '../../etc' and '<script>' return 400.
Request with a foreign Origin gets no CORS header.
31st Ask within 10 minutes returns 429 with Retry-After (tested with invalid questions so no tokens were spent).
Re-tested PDF extraction on unpdf 2.x: 473 pages in 3.4 s.
Page renders fully under the new Content-Security-Policy.

turns.prompt: Now test specifically for IDOR. List every route that takes an id or an object from the client, try to reach data the caller should not, and check whether shared caches can be poisoned across users.

turns.reply: No per-user data lives on the server, and caches are keyed by document URL or a hash of the full prompt, so they cannot be poisoned across users. One real weakness: the enrich endpoint trusted a whole filing object from the browser, so a caller could pair one company with another's filing or put their own text in front of the model. Fixed with a server-side lookup.
findings: /api/enrich accepted client-supplied title, summary, URL, category and ticker.
actions: store.js: getFiling(id).
push.js: enrichById(id, ticker) loads the filing from the store and verifies it belongs to that company.
Unknown id and mismatched company return the same 404, so ids cannot be enumerated; non-string ids rejected before any query.
Client sends only { id, ticker, read }.
verification: Own id + own company: 200.
Same id + another company: 404.
Made-up id: 404.
Object as id ({"$ne": null}): 400.
Old client-built filing object: 400.
No access code: 401.
